ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Assistance for national games 
*741. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister 
of YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) what monetary support and other facilities are given to a State for 
organising national and international games; 
(b) the assistance given and proposed to be given to Andhra Pradesh for 
preparation of the 32nd National Games 2002; 
(c) whether there is any proposal to ensure continued utilisation of sports 
equipment being procured; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SUSHREE 
UMA BHARTI): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) There is no provision in the existing schemes for providing 
monetary support and other facilities to a State for organising National and 
International Games as such. However, in the past, Government in relaxation of 
the provisions of the Scheme of Assistance to National Sports Federations, had 
provided financial assistance to State Governments for conduct of National 
Games and purchase of equipments. Besides this, Central assistance is 
provided for creation of sports facilities under the Scheme of "Grants for 
Creation of Sports Infrastructure" and "Grant for Installation of Synthetic 
Playing Surfaces" on receipt of viable proposals from State Governments. 
(b) Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh had requested for release of one-
time grant of Rs. 50.00 crores for creation of sports infrastructure for National 
Games to be held in Hyderbad during 2002. As no provision 

RAJYA SABHA [17 May, 2002] 
exists for providing ad-hoc or one time grant for creation of sports 
infrastructure, the Chief Minister was requested on 27-11-2001 to get suitable 
proposals for creation of sports infrastructure formulated in accordance with 
the prescribed norms in the Scheme for "Grants for Creation of Sports 
Infrastructure". 
(c) and (d) No such proposal has been received from the Government of 
Andhra Pradesh. However, the concerned State Government is supposed to 
ensure continued utilisation of sports equipments being procured by them. 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Sir, for the last two 
years, no National Games could be held. The Government of Andhra Pradesh, 
under the leadership of Shri Chandrababu Naidugaru came forward to conduct the 
Games, Sir, Andhra Pradesh has produced a number of champions in many 
fields, like badminton, wrestling and chess. Notable among them are 
Malleshwari in wrestling, who won the only Olympic^ Medal for India, in the 
last Olympic Games. Pullela Gopichand in badminton, Koneru Hampi and 
Harikrishna in chess. They have brought laurels to the country. The Government 
of Andhra Pradesh is encouraging sportsmen by giving incentives ranging from 
Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 25 lakhs. For conducting the Thirty-Second National Games, 
the Government of Andhra Pradesh is spending Rs.150 crores. So far, it has 
spent about Rs. 120 crores, by building seven huge stadia of high class standards. 
Sir, I request the Government of India to extend all financial help to the State 
Government for smooth conduct of the Games. 
My second request to the Government of India is to give exemption on 
customs and other duties on the import of sports material from Germany 
and other countries for this particular event.

Status of schemes under OBB and Education for All 
*744. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the details and the status of 'Operation Black Board' and 'Education for All' 
schemes under the Ministry; 
(b) the aims and objectives of these schemes under implementation by the 
Ministry; and 
(c) whether Government have achieved the desired goals? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) The Scheme of Operation Blackboard 
launched in 1987-1988 to improve facilities in primary schools of the country, 
provide for at least 2 reasonably large classrooms, at least 2 teachers and essential 
teaching learning material for every primary school existing on 30th September, 
1986. In 1993, the scope of Operation Blackboard was expanded to provide 
three teachers and three rooms to primary schools wherever enrolment exceeds 
100. The scheme was also extended to cover upper primary schools for Teaching 
Learning Equipment (TLE) and to provide an additional teacher. Under the Scheme 
funds have been provided to States for procurement of teaching and learning 
equipment to 522,902 primary schools and 138,009 upper primary schools. In 
all, 149,146 posts of additional teachers for converting single teacher primary 
schools into dual teacher school, 77,610 posts of additional teachers for upper 
primary schools and 83,045 posts of third teacher to primary schools with 
enrolment exceeding 100 children were sanctioned and also funds towards 
salary payment for all the new posts created were provided to the States. Provision 
for construction of school building was made under the 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [17 May, 2002] 
programmes of rural development on a sharing basis. In all 1.85 lakh 
additional classrooms have been constructed by States/UTs.The scheme of 
Operation Blackboard has been subsumed in the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan from the 
Tenth Five Year Plan. 
There is no scheme called 'Education for AH' being implemented by this 
Ministry. However, to realize the goals of Education for All, Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan, a national programme for uninversalization of elementary education has 
been launched with the objective of providing satisfactory quality education for 
all children in the age group 6—14 by 2010. The Scheme envisages 
preparation of District Elementary Education Plan (DEEP) by the States, 
reflecting community based habitation and village level planning. During 2001-
02 a sum of Rs. 1106.26 crore have been appwved for District Elementary 
Education Plans. 
Similarly, to achieve the goal to Education for All, the National Literacy 
Mission (NLM) seeks to impart functional literacy to non-literate in the 15—
35 age group. The objective is to attain a sustainable threshold level of 75 per 
cent literacy by 2005. The number of persons made literate till December 
31,2001 under all scheme of NLM is 9.66 crores. According to information 
received from the States, for the period 1996-97 to 2000-2001,60 per cent of 
those made literate were women, 21.23 per cent were scheduled castes and 11.79 
per cent were scheduled tribes. The total number of districts covered under the 
literacy programmes are 576. The effect of these programmes is evident from 
the fact that in the Census of 2001 the absolute number of illiterate persons has 
for the first time been reduced by 3.19 crores over a period of 10 years.

Curbing the use of pesticides 
5402. SHRI CO. POULOSE: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) Whether it is a fact that use of pesticides has gone up by several times 
in the last few decades; 
(b) whether Government have any information about the excessive use of 
pesticides in agriculture and allied production, food and food products; and 
(c) if so, the details of steps taken by Government to curb the unhealthy 
practice? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (c) Sir, though the 
consumption of pesticides increased from 54,775 Metric Tonne (Technical Grade) 
during 1980-81 to 75,033 Metric Tonne (Technical Grade) during 1990-1991, it 
considerably decreased to 43,584 Metric Tonne (Technical Grade) during 2000-
2001. 
Excessive use of pesticides in stray cases can take place because of ignorance 
of farmers. However, efforts are made for safe and judicious us of pesticides. If 
the pesticides are used as per the prescribed directions, they do not pose any harm 
to human beings, animals and the environment. The Government is promoting 
Integrated Pest Management (IPM) approach which inter alia comprises of cultural, 
mechanical and biological control in order to reduce the use of chemical 
pesticides in agriculture and allied sectors. 
In addition, following steps are taken by the Government to reduce 
excessive use of chemical pesticides in agriculture; 
(i) Training of farmers and extension officers through organization of 
Farmers' Field Schools; 
(ii) Establishement of State Biocontrol Laboratories for mass 
production of biocontrol agents and their field releases; 
(iii) Promotion of biopesticides like nuclear polyhedrosis virus, 
Bacillus thuringiensis and neem based biopesticides.

Impact of agricultural trade reforms on prices 
5407. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a survey conducted by the National Council on Applied 
Economic Research has indicated that agricultural trade reforms are likely to push 
up prices of cereals as compared to other grains; 
(b) whether the survey has also pointed out that this would adversely affect 
the poorer segments of both the rural and urban society; 
(c) if so, what are the other points made in the survey reports; 
(d) whether Government have considered the survey report; and 
(e) if so, what steps are being taken by Government in this regard? 
64 

[17 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRIHUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (e) National Council on Applied 
Economic Research (NCAER) has conducted a study on the likely impact of 
agriculture trade reforms on the consumption expenditure of the poor. 
Based on the nominal protection or effective protection co-efficients used in 
a study published in 1998, one of the findings of the present study is that trade 
liberalization in agriculture may lead to increase in prices of cereals and decline 
in prices of pulse, edible oil and arhar.This, according to the study may cause 
adverse impact on the poorer segment of the society. 
However, the conclusions in the study are based on the following 
assumption: 
1. Distribution of consumption expenditure across commodities is of the 
period 1994-95; 
2. Nominal or effective protection co-efficients are taken from a study 
published in 1998; and 
3. The results are based on partial equilibrium frame work which does 
not take into account income gains resulting from liberalization. 
The other main finding of the survey is that the role of Public Distribution 
System (PDS) may become more important in this scenario. 
As can be seen, this is a study constrained in its findings due to the 
overbearing assumptions. 
The, import of agricultural products is being closely monitored by the 
Government so that the trade- liberalization do not cause any adverse impact 
either on consumers or on producers. The Government has been undertakings 
various schemes in order to increase the production of cereals, pulses and 
oilseeds.

of the fact that crops and grown under rainfed condifions with no assured 
irrigation.

5417. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether experts have brough it to the notice of Government that certain 
aspects of globalisation are subjecting small and marginal farmers and farm

farming community? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRIHUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (c) India has been following the 
policy of economic liberalization since 1991 .There has been no unusual increase in 
imports except in edible oils, which has contributed to decline in prices of edible 
oils in domestic markets. In order to protect the interest of the famers market 
interventions are made to procure agricultural commodities covered under 
MSP Scheme and Market Intervention Scheme (MIS), if their prices fall.below 
MSP or the price fixed under MIS. The Government is implementing scheme 
for various cropss in which farmers including small and marginal farmers are 
given assistance of various types. The Government has been monitoring imports 
of sensitive agricultural commodities and takes action to regulate the import 
and, as and when necessary, import duties are increased.

of indebtedness has been carried out by National Sample Survey Organisation 
(NSSO), after 1992.Thus, it may not be possible to assess the increase or 
decrease of the same durinng the last decade during which liberalization has 
taken place. The Government has initiated a number of specific steps to 
reduce the indebtedness of farmers. These include introduction of crop 
insurance, re-scheduling of loans in events of natural calamity, and enhancing 
the profitability of agriculture through increase in productivity.

Regulation for Importing Soya Oil 
5420. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY:Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Ministry of Agriculture has laid down the rules stating that 
all imported Soyabean oil should be genetically non-modified. 
(b) if so, when these rules are likely to be enforced on consignments of 
imported Soya oil; 
(c) whether distinguishing the genetically modified soya oil from the 
conventional (non-modified) soya oil is immensely difficult through tests; and 
(d) if so, how Government propose to enforce the new regulations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) The Ministry of 
Agriculture has not laid down any guidelines/rules regarding import of 
genetically modified Soyabean oil. The import of genetically modified 
product is governed by Rules framed under Environment Protection Act, 1986 
which is handled by the Ministry of Environment and Forests. Rule 11 of the 
Rules for the Manufacture, Use, import, export and storage of Hazardous 
Micro-organisms/Genetically Engineered Organisms or Cells 1989 notified 
under EP Act 1986, provides that food stuffs, ingredient in food stuffs and 
additives including procesing aids containing or consisting of genetically 
engineered organisms or cells, shall not be produced, sold, imported or used 
except with approval of the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC). 
Distinction between genetically modified soyabean oil and non 
genetically modified soyabean oil is not possible by available analytical 
methods when the oils are refined. When oils are non refined very 
sophisticated and sensitive methods like Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) 
may enable the distinction. 
The GEAC is functioning under the Ministry of Environment and 
Forests to examine and issue clearance, on case to case basis, in proposals 
regarding production, sale, import or use of substances and products including 
food stuffs, ingredients in food stuffs and additives includding processing aids 
containing GM organisms. The GEAC takes decision after referring the 
proposals to experts and obtaining their views.

5437. DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: Will the Minister of

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Ministry of Environment and Forests have 
formulated National Forestry Action Programme (NFAP), a comprehensive 
strategic long term plan for the next twenty years to address the issues underlying 
major problems of the forestry sector in line with the National Forest Policy, 
1988. The objective of the NFAP is to bring one-third area of the country under 
forest/tree cover and to arrest de-forestation for achieving sustainable 
development of forests. 
The National Forestry Action Programme has five main components: 
1. Protect Existing Forest Resources: It has three main-sub programmes 
(i) Forest protection, (ii) Soil and water conservation, and (iii) Protected areas 
and bio-diversity conservation. 
2. Improve Forest Productivity: It has four main sub-programmes (i) 
Rehabilitation of degraded forest, (ii) Research and technology development, 
(iii) Development of Non-Wood Forest Products, and (iv) Assisting private 
initiatives with community participation. 
3. Reduce Total Demand: It has three main sub-programmes for efficient 
uses (i) Fuelwood and fodder, (ii) Timber, and (iii) Non-Wood Forest Products.

programmes, (i) Central forestry administration, (ii) Central forestry 
institutions, and (iii) State forestry administration and institutions. 
5. Expand Forest Area: It has two main sub-programmes (i) Tree 
plantation on forest and non-forest lands, and (ii) People's participation in 
plantations and their protection.

(a) whether the Supreme Court, while strongly indicating the Union 
Government in the CNG case, drew their attention to the increase in 
respiratory diseases among children; 
(b) if so, whether the Court also pointed out that it has been the concern 
of the Union Government in this regard; 
100 

[17 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether the Supreme Court has also warned the Union Government and the 
health authorities to take appropriate action and arrest air pollution; and 
(d) if so, what is the reaction of Government? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R 
BAALU): (a) to (d) The Supreme Court in its order dated 5th April, 2002, in 
respect of a Writ Petition (Civil) No. 13029 of 1985 M.C.Mehta Vs. Union of India 
and Others has referred to the reports of the Central Pollution Control Board and 
other reports on environmental pollution and consequent health effects including 
non-compliance with environmental standards.The Apex Court expressed its concern 
over the deterioration of air quality and its impact on health in some cities. The steps 
taken by the Government to control pollution include the following: 
(i) The Ministry of Environment and Forest constituted a Committee on 
Environment and Health to develop appropriate policy, strategy and action 
plan regarding environmental health. The report of the Committee has been 
accepted by the Government. As a follow up of the recommendations, 
an Environmental Health Cell has been constituted and a number of 
environmental health studies have been commissioned to generate the data 
case. 
(ii) A Comprehensive Policy for abatement of pollution w: tya 
stress on the preventive and control a°.oects of pollution has been 
evolved. 
(iii) Emission standards for on-road vehicles and mass emission standards for new 
vehicles have been notified under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and are 
enforced by the Transport Departments of the State Governments 
including Delhi. 
(iv) Unleaded petrol is supplied in the entire country from 1.2.2000 and diesel 
with 0.25% sulphur maximum content is supplied from 1.1.2000 in the entire 
country. Ultra low sulphur (0.05%) fuel has also been introduced in 
major cities. 
(v) Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) is supplied to automobiles through a number 
of retail outlets in Delhi and Mumbai to cater to the CNG vehicles. 
(vi) Benzene content in petrol has been reduced. 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [17 May, 2002] 
(vii) A network of 295 Ambient Air Quality and 507 Ambient Water 
Quality Monitoring Stations have been set up throughout the 
country. 
(viii) Emission standards for industries have been notified under the 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to check pollution. 
(ix) Steps have been taken to control pollution from 17 categories of highly 
polluting industries. 
(x) Industries are also required to provide necessary pollution control 
measures before commissioning of their plants. 
(ix) Industries are required to take consent from the respective State 
Pollution Control Board under the Water (Prevention and Control of 
Pollution) Act, 1974, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 
1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 for discharging 
their effluent and hazardous waste. 
(xii) Environmental Action Plans for 24 critically polluted areas have been 
prepared and are under implementation.

5460. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

in Bangalore on the 10th December, 2001;

Tenth Five Year Plan towards a gender sensitive and people-centred plan with 
focus on decentralised empowerment of communities, concentrating on 
grassroot level participation;

(d) whether Government have considered these suggestions; and

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATISUMITRA MAHAJAN) (a) Yes,

Development, the World Bank had organised the Southern Regional Consultation 
Meet for Engendering the Tenth Five Year Plan at Bangalore on 10-11 
December, 2001. 
(b) and (c) The Workshop made a number of recommendations on 
education, health, employment and anti-poverty schemes for women as also on 
gender mainstreaming of governance and the convergence of services at the 
grassroot level. 
(d) and (e) Planning Commission is using these recommendations 
alongwith recommendations of other Working Groups, for the preparation of the 
Tenth Five Year Plan.

Programme delivers an integrated package of basic services including 
supplementary nutrition, pre-school education, immunization, health check 
up, referral services, and nutrition and health education.The Reproductive 
and Child Health Programme was launched in 1997 for providing child

Amendment) Bill, 2001 has the objective of making education of all 
children in the age group of 6—14 years a fundamental right. The

monitor proper implementation of existing laws for children and protection

167

consider setting up glaciology study/research centres, on the lines of 
Glaciology Research Centre, Moscow and Lanzhon Institute of Glaciology and 
Geocryology, China; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) to (c) Yes. The 
Department of Science and Technology had initiated a multi-disciplinary and 
multi-institutional nationally coordinated programme on Himalayan 
Glaciology in the early eighties of the last century so as to create a strong R&D 
base in the country for studying the different aspects of Himalayan Glaciers 
including snow melt run-off and mass balance studies. Under this programme 
several specific research projects, including multi-institutional and multi-
disciplinary field observations have been funded. 
Geological Survey of India has also been carrying out studies on 
Himalayan Glaciers, including field surveys. 
The studies carried our under these programmes so far have indicated that the 
glaciers in the Himalayan region are passing through a phase of recession. The 
recession of glaciers is a natural process sensitive to climatic fluctuation 
wherein the rise in global average temperature (called global warming) results in 
melting of the glaciers in extents varying with their locations as well as 
seasons. 
As far as resultant threat of global warming to Himalayan Glaciers is 
concerned neither enough data nor empirical evidence that links global 
warming to the melting of the Himalayan Glacier is available. 
In order togather long time series data needed to understand vario JS 
glaciological processes, a multi-disciplinary and multi-institutionally 
coordinated field-observation based R&D programme in Gangotri region has 
been recently launched. 
A proposal has also been formulated to set up in the country a National 
Centre for Field Operations and Research on Himalayan Glaciology (NCFOR-
HG).The Proposal forms a part of the 10th Plan Programme of Department of 
Science andTechnolgy.The proposed centre would provide

administrative infrastructure! and technical support to glaciological studies in the

Research activities in Antarctic Region 
5511. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: 
Will the Minister of OCEAN DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
173 

RAJYA SABHA [17 May, 2002] 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government propose to enhance research 
activities at Antarctic Station; 
(b) if so, what are the new activities proposed to be taken up; and 
(c) what are the achievements made during the last three years in 
Antarctic Research Programme? 
THE MINISTER OF OCEAN DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. The scientific activities are 
proposed to be enhanced/initiated at Indian Station during the XXII Indian 
Antarctic Expedition. They are, use of Multi Scanning Multispectral 
Radiometer data to study the changes in ice cover over Antarctic region 
especially around Indian Station and assessment of ice sheet thickness using 
Ground Penetrating Radar to undertake ice core drilling. The ice core studies 
are useful to understand paleo-climate of Antractica. 
(c) Achievements made during 1998-99 (18th Expedition) were: 
installation of Brewer spectrophotometer to measure total ozone, SO2, NO2 and 
UV; mapping of intensity of seasonal variation of geomagnet c field and total 
magnetic field; installation of two Automatic Weather Station with DCP; 
recording of 360 seismic events using digital seismometer integrated with 
GPS; recording of lateral plate movements on mm scale using GPs; recording 
of various surface energy flux on an annual basis with energy loss estimated as 
45 W/sqm and installation of two prototype wind machines. 
Achievements made during 1999-2000 (19th Expedition) were: 
launching of expedition from South Africa for first time resulting into 
operational, scientific and economic gains; real time analysis of VLF 
Whistlers; establishment of permanent environmental lab at Maitri; detection 
of waste water contamination of permafrost; recording of presence of exogenous 
pollen grains on lake sediments dated back to 10000 years; interfacing of seismic 
station with international Antarctic network and recording of several new 
species of low grade flora and fauna. 
Achievements made during 2000-2001 (20th Expedition) were: 
establishment of a 3-station triangulation experiment and simultaneous 
magnetic recording to understand the dynamics of the auroral current 
systems; measurement of atmospheric electrical parameters near the Kamat 
Hut at Maitri to study the global electric circuit; continuous 
174 

[17 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
observation on the weather pattern, atmospheric pressure, surface ozone and global 
solar radiation at Maitri; continuous recording of VLF propagation data by digital 
audio recorder PCM-R300 and geological mapping in the Muhlig-
Hoffmannfjell area which revealed charnockite. The snow grain identification 
studies indicated predominantly sugary grains at Veteiah, Shivling and 
Russian Aerodrome site.

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
PLIGHT OF TEMPORARY WORKERS OF PRAGA TOOLS LIMITED 
SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY (West Bengal): Sir, I wish to draw the 
attention of the Government to the plight of nearly 200 temporary employees, 
as recognised by the Deputy Commissioner of Labour, Andhra Pradesh, 
belonging to both technical as well as non-technical category, working in M/s. 
Praga Tools Limited, which is a subsidiary of a public sector enterprise, 
namely, H.M.T. It is situated at Kavadiguda Road, Secunderabad, Andhra 
Pradesh. 
In spite of their putting in nearly 10 to 12 years of service, the 
Management of the Praga Tools Limited is treating them as casual workers, 
and, thus, depriving them of VRS. 
Due to irregular payment of wages, these employees and their 
families are almost on the verge of starvation. Besides that, the threat of 
closure of this company is also weighing heavily on the minds of these 
Workers. The VRS announced by the Government is applicable only to 
permanent employees, Badili workers, and work-charged and temporary 
employees. These casual employees, most of whom have crossed 40 years of 
age, are willing to leave the company by taking VRS. But the management is 
not considering their request. 
Under these circumstances, the Government of India should take 
immediate steps to treat these casual employees of the Praga Tools Limited, 
who have put in more than 10 to 12 years of service, as temporary employees 
and extend the benefits of VRS to them. In the meanwhile, steps should be 
taken to disburse wages to them, including arrears, for the survival of their 
families during these hard days. 
SHRI SK. KHABIR UDDIN AHMED (West Bengal): Sir, I 
associate myself with it. 
POOR FACILITIES AT ARIYALUR RAILWAY STATION OF 
SOUTHERNRAILWAY 
SHRI S. SIVASUBRAMANIAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I would like to 
bring to the notice of this august House the plight of a railway station in my 
State. 
Ariyalur railway station, since 1880, is located under the 
administrative control of Trichy Railway Division, Southern Railway.    The 
198 

[17   May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
station caters to the needs of the public of Perambalur district. Express trains, 
Vaigai Express, Pandian Express, Pallavan Express, Rock Fort Express stop 
at this station. Thousands of rail users use this station daily for boarding and 
alighting. It is an important station. But, provision of a food/tea stall is 
missing. The passengers need the facility for taking snacks and tea/coffee. 
Provision of a food/tea stall in the Ariyalur railway station will take care of 
better passenger amenities. 
The pathway is much lower than the platform. This results in 
injuries to passengers, who get down from the platform. If the pathway is 
laid, it will avoid injuries to the users. This will take care of the safety of 
thousands of passengers, who use the railway facilities every day. 
Sir, I hope the Railway Minister will accede to the requests which I 
have raised.  Thank you.

FORCIBLE ACQUISITION OF SC/ST LANDS BY MAHANADI 
COALFIELDS LTD. ORISSA 
DR. M.N. DAS (Orissa): Sir, in 1974-75, the Government of Orissa 
distributed land to the landless Scheduled Castes people in several backward 
areas. These people developed their plots, and started cultivation on that land, 
on the right of holding pattas. Usually, these people are too backward to 
understand their legal rights, or, even to raise their voice against injustices 
inflicted on them. Taking advantage of their ignorance and extreme poverty, 
the Mahanadi Coalfields Limited, a public sector company, started forcible 
acquisition of their land under provisions of the Coal-bearing (Acquisition 
and Development) Act of 1957. Though the Act provides for acquisition, the 
Mahanadi Coalfields Limited authorities, in violation of that law, have taken 
possession of the dalit and tribal lands for the purpose of expansion. The 
company did not serve any notice on the tribal people, no compensation was 
announced, and no rehabilitation measures were undertaken and the people 
were just taken for a ride. It is just like exploiting the dumb and mute people. 
The MCL has resorted to illegal mining activities, without humanitarian 
consideration. Of late, 300 acres of land has already been forcibly acquired in 
the IB-valley area from the dalits and tribals, because the area is remote and 
the people are too ignorant. While exploration of mines is necessary for 
economic development of the region, it is also imperative on the part of the 
MCL to strictly follow the rules and regulations. It should not play with the 
lives and livelihood of the innocent people. I appeal to the Union Government 
to look into the irregularities committed by the Mahanadi Coalfields Limited 
in Orissa.

SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION 
The Dastardly Attack by Terrorists on Civilians and Army Personnel and 
their Family Memebrs in Jammu and Kashmir on 14th May, 2002 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Mr. Vice-Chairman, 
Sir, thank you for giving me this opportunity for raising a discussion under 
rule 176 on the dastardly attack by terrorists on civilians and army personnel 
in Jammu and Kashmir on the 14th May, 2002, leading to the killing of a large 
number of persons including women and children, its implications and the 
response of the Government thereto. Words are not enough to condemn this 
barbarism, this heinous crime. The anguish and the sense of outrage felt across 
the length and breadth of the country cannot be expressed in languages. Sir, 
the purpose of raising this discussion is not to score some debating points here 
and there, but to reflect our collective anguish and outrage, and to facilitate the 
Government to formulate its views, formulate its actions, after hearing the 
views of the representatives of the people, representing the cross-section of 
this country. Sir, on the 14" 1 of May. in the evening, the hon. Home Minister 
expressed his sadness while informing the House about this attack. This latest 
attack by the terrorists raises certain questions, and we shall have to respond 
collectively to those questions. This is not the first; rather, this is the latest in 
the series of these types of acts, and it is part of the proxy war that has been 
going on, in the name of terrorist activities, in the State of Jammu and 
Kashmir. It is really unprecedented because of its depth and magnitude. 
Sir, coming to seizures, I will give you just one figure about the arms 
and ammunition seized over a period of ten years, from May, 1990 to April, 
2000. 33,763 weapons of various calibre, three million rounds of ammunition, 
1,22,332 explosive devices, and a large volume of other war materials were 
seized. That is the magnitude of the attack, and that is the depth of the attack, 
that is taking place. It is a cold reality that Pakistan considers that its dream of 
Two-Nation Theory' remains unrealised unless they are in a position to annex 
Kashmir.   To pursue that line, they launched 
232 

[17th May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
regular wars on three occasions, and the fourth one was the intrusion in 
Kargil. These facts are known to all of us. I am not going to narrate the 
history. The moot point with which we are confronted today is, how we are 
going to respond. Is the global alliance that has been formed after the 
September 11 attack on the World Trade Centre in USA, and that has led to 
the destruction of the Taliban regime in Afghanistan, going to take note of 
our concerns, and is this alliance going to help us in our battle against 
terrorism? We were encouraged when we were told by the Leader of the 
House, and the Minister in charge of External Affairs, Shri Jaswant Singh, on 
the floor of this very House, that we will be a beneficiary; the Taliban regime 
in Afghanistan has done nothing else but manufacture terrorism, and 
terrorism alone; if that factory manufacturing terrorism, of which we have 
been the victims, is being destroyed, we are going to be a beneficiary. But it 
is a hard fact now that we have not been a beneficiary. The ground reality is 
that there is a categorisation of terrorist activities. There are some acts for 
which global action is called for; there are some other terrorist activities 
which do not attract that type of attention! This is the hard reality now. 
Otherwise, how does one justify that you are fighting terrorism by co-opting a 
country which has accepted terrorism as a State policy? How do you expect 
that that alliance is going to take note of our concerns? I am afraid, we are 
expecting too much. Perhaps, a time has come when we shall have to 
recognise the fact that this is a battle which we shall have to fight on our own. 
How can we fight this battle? Various formulations and ideas are floated. First 
of all, the Government of the day has to make a hard assessment on the basis 
of the facts and information available to them. Nobody else can do it; the 
Government, the Government of the day alone can do it, because our 
information is limited; our assessment may not be perfect. We need not 
necessarily react like knee-jerk reaction; we need not necessarily react only in 
words which, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, are unfortunately happening. 
On 14th of December, after the attack on Parliament House itself, it 
was decided by the entire political establishment of this country that we must 
convey a message, the "message should be clear and loud that democratic 
institutions in this country are most important, political establishment of this 
country, irrespective of their individual creed, faith and belief are united, in 
conveying this message in clear and loud terms, that we refuse to succumb to 
the pressure and bullying tactics of terrorist activities. Next day, the 
Parliament met; next day, our resolve to fight against terrorism was 
pronounced clearly and loudly. Six months have passed! How did we

RAJYA SABHA [17th May, 2002] 
translate that resolve into action? This is the question which we shall have to 
answer it. If we expect, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, that somebody else will fight 
our battle, I am afraid, we are sadly mistaken. Yes, we may draw some 
comfort from expressing sympathy and concern from some high-ups of our 
friendly countries. 
Sir, I was just going through an interview given by the visiting U.S.

matter, the global alliance, led by the United States of America is going to 
help us? Whatever be the perception of the Government, but the 
developments of the last six months have clearly demonstrated that it did not 
have any impact at all on policy makers of Pakistan. If there was a statement

don't know how we are going to tackle the problem.

on the civilians as well as the military personnel on 14 th May. I find great 
symbolism in this discussion because this discussion signifies the battle of the 
civilized world with the barbaric terrorism of a few. As a matter of fact, this 
terrorism is an anti-civilisation war which is making it more symbolic by 
attacking the Jammu and Kashmir Assembly, the Indian Parliament and then 
the military personnel time and again. I find that this is a vibrant democracy 
which is responding to the challenge by demonstrating, firstly,, the solidarity 
of the people represented by us, and secondly, by the resolve of the 
Government to meet the challenge. Sir, Kaluchak became Kaal-incarnate to 
those who suffered at the hands of the Fidayeens who came here to kill and 
die. Those people who send these Fidayeens to this country have scant respect 
for humanity is apparent because those who come here to kill know that they 
are going to die here only and they meet that fate. But at what cost? The 
human cost is something which they do not comprehend which makes us 
sadder and sadder. If war is, many a time, described as politics by other 
means, the terrorism which we are facing is, in a way war, by other means. 
Sometimes, it is called a proxy war. America, on many occasions, guides the 
world discourse, and, therefore, we are told that some wars are of high 
intensity and some wars are of low intensity and the Americans are not in a 
position to place this war in their categorisation. But this is a war, which is our 
experience. America has formed a coalition against terrorism after n m 
September. But we were already at war. The statistics have come before the 
House probably during this Session only. During the last few years we have 
spent Rs. 45,000 crores; we have lost 60,000 civilians; we have lost 8,000 
security personnel and 48,000 kilogram of RDX have been seized. All these 
statistics are there on the record of this House. But this war is costing us like 
anything. We are appalled when we see that the war. is being waged by those 
who claim to be partners in the world coalition against terrorism. I do not 
know whether you call this a paradox or an irony. Can we call this a classic 
case of 'running with the hare and hunting with

DR. V. MAITREYAN (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Vice Chairman, Sir, the 
horrendous and barbaric attack on an army camp, and on tourists, near 
Jammu on 14 th May, 2002, has to be condemned by one and all, in the 
strongest way possible. On behalf of my Party, and on behalf of the people of 
Tamil Nadu, I offer my heartfelt condolences to the members of the bereaved 
families. The identification of the three terrorists, who were killed, as 
Pakistani nationals, only confirms the role of Pakistan. Pakistan has been 
brazenly waging a proxy-war on India by promoting cross-border terrorism. 
After the September 11, 2001, attack on the World Trade Centre in 
USA, there was a global initiative to fight terrorism. But Pakistan has been 
violating this initiative, with impunity. There was an attack on the State 
Assembly of Srinagar on October 1, 2001, in which 38 persons were killed, 
and 60 others injured. Then, there was the attack within the premises of 
Parliament House, New Delhi, on December 13, 2001. Then, there was the 
attack on the American Centre in Kolkatta on January 22, 2002. This was 
followed by the terrorists' attack on the Raghunath Temple in Jammu in 
April, 2002, and, now, there is this major onslaught at Kaluchak. 
During these eight months. India had taken several diplomatic 
initiatives. It had mobilised international opinion against Pak-sponsored 
cross-border terrorism. But Pakistan has been continuing its proxy-war 
against India, undeterred. There has been a continuation of such attacks since 
September 11, up till May 14, 2002.

We want to know from the Government where is the political will? 
Have you shown any political will in the past four years to stamp our 
terrorism? That is the second point that I wanted to make. The third point that 
I want to make is about what happened on 14 th of May. That is very 
interesting. Some answer must come from the Government. On the 14 th of 
May, when terrorists alighted from the bus and killed seven passengers in the 
bus, they ran towards the camp, which was the area of the 196 Artilery Unit of 
the Army. They crossed over the boundary wall and then laid booby traps.

houses of various innocent families and Army Officers and killed twenty-
seven people at random. By the time help arrived, it was I0.30.a.m. The attack 
started at 6.20 a.m. and help arrived at 10.30 a.m. Facts may be wrong, facts 
may be incorrect. I do not know. Therefore, the Government must explain 
about the time factor involved. All this information I got from newspaper 
reports. 
The fourth point I want to mention is that we, as a nation, are in very 
peculiar position. I remember in Burk ino Faso, when Narasimha Raoji was 
the Prime Minister, he had made a statement on Jammu and Kashmir. Let me 
quote him. He said, "We cannot, therefore, be mute the spectators to their 
sufferings." He was talking about the sufferings of the people of Jammu and 
Kashmir. This was on 4th November, 1995. Now, we are in 2002 and the same 
language is being stated. I do not want to blame any political party. Now, the 
pharse we are using is: "We are running out of patience."   It is the same 
pharse.   "How long will we be mute spectators?"

jungle still prevails, no matter how civilised the countries may have become.

RESOLUTION CONDEMNING DASTARDLY ATTACK BY 
TERRORISTS AT KALUCHAK, JAMMU ON 14™ MAY, 2002 
THE VICE CHAIRMAN (SHRI SURESH PACHOURI): I now move 
the following Resolution: 
"This House strongly condemns th e most dastardly attack at 
Kaluchak, Jammu on 14 th May, 2002 by terrorists belonging to Lakshar-e-
Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammad from across Pakistan and conveys its heartfelt 
sympathies to the bereaved families. 
We have consistently tried to build friendly relations with Pakistan 
through the mechanisms provided by Shimla Agreement and Lahore 
Declaration to solve all existing problems. But to our great disappointment, 
our efforts did not meet with the desired response from Pakistan. 
It is essential that the leaders of the world community take note of 
the continuing acts of terrorism encouraged by Pakistan so that united and 
effective action can be taken against the same. 
The House resolves to fight against such senseless acts of terrorism 
which are against humanity as a whole in a united and determined manner 
and declares this Nation's commitment to see an end to this menace." 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SURESH PACHOURI) : May I 
take it that this Resolution is adopted unanimously?

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRi SURESH PACHOURI): The 
Budget Session commenced on Monday, the 26 ,h February, 2002 with the 
President's Address to both the Houses of Parliament. 
We have had 38 sittings spread over around 160 hours, with a 
Budget break in between. The House sat late on some occasions beyond 
normal working time for more than 25 hours to complete legislative and other 
important business. However, more than 50 hours were spent over the 
Ayodhya issue, storming of the Orissa State Legislature by a mob and the 
issue of violence in Gujarat. 
During the Session, 60 (50 newly-elected and 10 re-elected) 
Members made and subscribed oath/affirmation and took their seats in the 
House. During the Session, we condoled the death of eight former Members 
as well as the death of Shri G.M.C. Balayogi. Speaker, Lok Sabha, and Shri 
Daya Nand Sahay, a sitting Member of this House under tragic circumstances. 
During the Session, 175 Reports of various Parliamentary 
Committees were presented or laid on the Table of the House. During the 
Session, substantial Government Legisl ative Business was transacted for a 
total period of 46 hours, 6 new Bills were introduced and 3 Bills were 
withdrawn. 36 Bills were passed; out of which 11 were financial Bills, 2 Bills 
were repealing Bills, 3 were new Bills and 20 Bills were amending Bills, 
including the Constitution (93rd) Amendment Bill, 2001, which seeks to insert 
Article 21A in the Constitution as Fundamental Right to provide for free and 
compulsory education to children between 6 years and 14 years of age. 
The Statutory Resolution on POTO seeking its disapproval was 
adopted and motion for consideration of the Prevention of Terrorism Bill was 
defeated. The Prevention of Terrorism Bill, 2002, (known as POTO), was 
finally passed by both the Houses at a Joint sitting on the 26 th March, 2002, 
third in the history of Parliament. 
There were 11 Statements by Ministers. Prominent among them were 
(a) on the issue of current situation in Ayodhya in the wake of Supreme 
Court's judgment (by the Prime Minister); (b) on the recently concluded 
Commonwealth Summit in Australia; (c) revision in the 5 prices of domestic 
L.P.G.; (d) on the National Tourism Policy, 2002 and (e) terrorist

attack on the bus passengers and at army camp at Kaluchak near Jammu; 
which occasioned a number of clarifications being sought by Members. 
We had one Calling Attention on the Securities Scam in Cooperative 
Banks and failure of the Central Government Regulators which occasioned a 
number of clarifications being sought by Members. 
We had Short Duration Discussions on the following 4 subjects 
which lasted for more than 15 hours:- 
I. Grave situation created by continuing violence in the State 
of Gujarat resulting in the loss of a large number of 
innocent lives and property; 
II. Role of Governors in discharging their constitutional 
responsibilities in the formation of Governments in States 
in the light of recent events in Uttar Pradesh; 
III. Drinking water crisis in the country;  and 
IV. Dastardly attack by terrorists on civilians and army 
personnel and their family members in Jammu and Kashmir 
on 14"1 May, 2002 leading to the killing of a large number 
of persons including women and children. 
There were about 130 Special Mentions on Matters of Public 
Importa/ice. Members will agree that this device is now becoming a very 
useful means of raising issues of public importance and ensuring the 
accountability of Government. 
The House discussed at length a Motion expressing its deep sense of 
anguish at the persistence of violence in Gujarat and urging the Central 
Government to intervene effectively under Article 355 of the Constitution to 
protect the lives and properties of the citizens and to provide effective relief 
and rehabilitation to the victims of violence. The Motion was unanimously 
adopted after a long and sometimes heated debate spread over three days and 
which lasted for more than 18 hours. Hon. Chairman also congratulated the 
House for adopting the above Motion on Gujarat unanimously and hoped that 
this will usher in an era of lasting peace for the people of Gujarat.

The House also adopted a Resolution moved by the Leader of the 
House, Shri Jaswant Singh, expressing its deep concern and anguish over the 
storming of the estate and precincts of the State Legislature of Orissa by a 
mob of persons. 
During the Session, General and Railway Budgets were discussed 
along with their Appropriation Bills which lasted for more than eight hours. 
During the Session, the working of three Ministries, namely, Labour, External 
Affairs and Agriculture, was discussed, which lasted for more than twelve 
hours. However, the discussion on the working of the Ministry of Agriculture 
remained inconclusive. 
Four important matters -- (a) the situation in Ayodhya; (b) 
commemoration of the centenary year of Anushilan Samiti ; (c) purchasing of 
Coffins/Caskets at a higher price during the Kargil War; and (d) alleged 
supply of election material to the Finance Minister in 1999 by the Chairman 
of a company, which is under CBI investigation-- were raised with the 
permission of the hon. Chairman, the discussion on which lasted for more 
than two hours. 
During the Session, 759 Starred questions and 5519 Unstarred 
Questions -were admitted and answered. Of these, 84 Starred Questions were 
orally answered, and 7 Statements by Ministers, correcting the answers to 
questions were laid/made. 
During the Session, three References were made by the hon. 
Chairman regarding (a) the International Women's Day; (b) the violence that 
took place within the sacred precincts of the Sabarmati Ashram in Gujarat, 
which was the Headquarters of Gandhiji, the Father of the Nation; and (c) the 
Fiftieth Anniversary of Rajya Sabha. 
On the occasion of the Fiftieth Anniversary of Parliament of India, a 
new Parliament Library Building (Sansadiya Gyanpeeth) was inaugurated and 
dedicated to" the nation by the President of India on the 7th May, 2002. 
I would like to take this opportunity to thank the Leader of the 
House, the Leader of the Opposition, the leaders of various Parties/Groups 
and all the hon. Members for the kind co-operation extended by them in 
conducting the proceedings of the House.
